parent.name: Bird Opening: Dutch Variation
parent.overview: After 1.f4 d5 the game resembles a Dutch Defence with colours reversed and White a tempo up. White's main aims are control of e5 and the dark central squares with the f-pawn, usually 2.Nf3 followed either by a g3/Bg2 fianchetto or by e3, Be2, O-O and d3 or d4/c3 (Stonewall formation). Black meets it by fighting for the centre and the dark squares: a fianchetto with ...g6/...Bg7, or ...Nf6, ...e6 and ...c5, with ...Bg4 as a pin. The play is positional and both sides develop to optimal squares; the downside of f4 is a weakened kingside, so it is 'double-edged' for less experienced players. Sources say there is little theory, it can be a surprise weapon at club level, and the opening has been tried by strong players (Larsen, Carlsen, Nakamura, Karjakin) but is not popular at the top, with White scoring only about 46.7% overall.

parent.name: King's Indian Attack
parent.overview: White builds the mirror image of the King's Indian Defence: Nf3, g3, Bg2, O-O, d3, Nbd2 and e4, usually against any Black set-up, particularly ...d5 with ...e6 or ...c5. The central pawn push e4-e5 gives a kingside bind and space, after which White expands with h4-h5, g4 and knight manoeuvres (Nf1-e3/g3 or Ne1-g2) towards a kingside attack. Black generally seeks counterplay on the queenside with ...c5, ...b5 or ...a5, or contests e4 directly. It has a modest theory load and keeps the same ideas whatever Black plays, so it is popular at club level, though it is uncommon among top grandmasters today. Black's main dilemma is that passive play lets White have a superior version of the King's Indian Defence, while ...e5 can leave Black behind in development.

root.name: Van Geet Opening: Hergert Gambit
root.moves: 1. Nc3 d6 2. f4 e5 3. fxe5 Nc6

parent.name: Van Geet Opening
parent.overview: White develops a knight to c3, controlling e4 and d5, and keeps the pawn structure undecided to choose a set-up once Black replies. The knight blocks the c-pawn, so Queen's Gambit and English structures are not available without reorganising. Main replies: 1...d5 (the cleanest; 2.e4 transposes to obscure Scandinavian lines, or the Van Geet Attack after 2...d4 3.Nce2), 1...e5 (then 2.e4 Vienna Game, the most common transposition in the database, or 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.d4 Napoleon Attack), 1...Nf6 (one of the most unpleasant replies for White) and 1...c5 (transposing to Closed Sicilian or inferior-placed-knight lines). Sources call it sound and low-theory but unambitious: Black equalises with accurate play, so it earns points from surprise rather than from an edge, and masters play it under 1% of the time, though some strong correspondence players use it. The database root has few games itself; most of the subtree (about 290M games) is Vienna, Closed Sicilian and Chigorin-style transpositions that play like those openings.

parent.name: Caro-Kann Defense
parent.overview: Black plays ...c6 to support ...d5 and so challenges the e4 pawn with a sound pawn structure, while keeping the light-squared bishop free to come out to f5 or g4 before ...e6 (the French Defence's main drawback, at the cost of a tempo). Black accepts less space early and tends to get a resilient, hard-to-break structure with few weaknesses and good endgame prospects. Play is mostly positional and manoeuvring; it is called more solid and less dynamic than the Sicilian (s1). The Advance (3.e5 Bf5) and Panov-Botvinnik (3.exd5 cxd5 4.c4) lines are more combative, and the Advance became the most popular White try in the 21st century. Main branches: Classical (4...Bf5), Advance, Exchange, Panov, 4...Nf6 lines, Gurgenidze (...g6), Two Knights (2.Nc3 d5 3.Nf3) and Fantasy (3.f3). This is a crossroads root after 1...c6; the pawn structures differ by branch.

parent.name: Ruy Lopez: Morphy Defense
parent.moves: 1. e4 e5 2. Nf3 Nc6 3. Bb5 a6 4. Ba4 Nf6 5. O-O d6
parent.overview: 3...a6 is the main road of the Ruy Lopez (roughly two thirds to 90 per cent of Ruy games per the sources). It asks White's bishop an immediate question: Bxc6 (Exchange) or the retreat 4.Ba4, after which Black can play ...b5 to kick the bishop again. The main line is the Closed Ruy (5.O-O Be7 6.Re1 b5 7.Bb3 d6 8.c3 O-O 9.h3), a locked, slow centre where White builds the c3-d4 pawn duo and reroutes the knight Nb1-d2-f1-g3, and Black seeks queenside counterplay with ...c5/...c4 or ...Bb7 and ...Re8/...Bf8. Alternatives at move five or later include the Open Variation (5...Nxe4), the Arkhangelsk (5...b5), and Marshall Attack (8...d5), with Anti-Marshall systems used by White to dodge it. Play is typically slow positional manoeuvring (the 'Spanish torture': a small White edge pressed for forty moves) with very deep theory. It has been a main weapon of nearly every world champion.

parent.name: Vienna Game
parent.overview: White develops the queen's knight before the king's knight, protecting e4 and adding a second guard of d5, and keeps the f-pawn free. That flexibility is the point: White can later play f4 for a delayed King's Gambit (the Vienna Gambit), develop the bishop with 3.Bc4 for an Italian or Bishop's Opening structure (with the Qg4 raid against ...Bc5 and the Frankenstein-Dracula after ...Nxe4), or fianchetto with 3.g3 for a quieter game. Black usually answers 2...Nf6 (the Falkbeer, about 60 percent in one source) or 2...Nc6, and the standard equaliser is a timely ...d5. Theory leaves the opening objectively equal, with little elite use but a lot of club use; it is a surprise weapon that avoids the heavily prepared Spanish and Italian lines. The root is a family, so its character depends on White's third move.

parent.name: Hungarian Opening
parent.overview: White plays 1.g3 to fianchetto the king's bishop to g2 and hit the long diagonal, deferring any central commitment (s1, s3). It is a flank opening that usually transposes: into the King's Indian Attack (Nf3, d3, O-O, then e4), the Catalan, the Réti or the English, depending on Black's set-up (s1, s3, s4). Black can happily occupy the centre with ...d5 or ...e5, or choose Sicilian, Caro-Kann or King's Indian-style set-ups (s2, s3). Positions are usually closed or flexible, with long-term strategic play rather than early tactics (s1, s3). Engines and statistics find it essentially equal, with White at most slightly more comfortable (s3, s4). Theory is minimal: it is closer to a move order than a distinct variation (s2).
